subtitle: Fraud Protection
description: Scammers are getting smarter. But now, so are you. This chapter is your armor -- learn to spot, dodge, and report the tricks that cost Indians Rs 7,000+ crore every year.

data.content: Here is a number that should make you sit up: Indians lost **Rs 7,061 crore** to cyber fraud in just six months of 2024. That is enough to buy roughly 14,000 brand-new cars. And these were not all gullible people -- engineers, doctors, IIT grads, senior executives. Smart people. People just like your parents. People just like you will be.

data.text: Wait, hold on. If smart people fall for scams too, then what even makes a scam work? Like, why do people just... hand over their money?

data.content: That is the million-rupee question. And the answer is not 'because people are stupid.' The answer is because scammers have figured out your brain's shortcuts. Once you understand those shortcuts, you become nearly impossible to fool.

Scammers do not win because they are geniuses. They win because they know which buttons to press in your brain -- the same buttons that helped your ancestors run from tigers. Let us learn what those buttons are, so nobody presses them on you.

Every successful scam -- from a Rs 500 fake lottery to a Rs 2,000 crore Ponzi scheme -- runs on the same three-legged stool. Remove one leg and the whole thing collapses. Those three legs? **Fear**, **Greed**, and **Urgency**.

data.definition: Manipulating people psychologically to make them give up money or sensitive information. No hacking required -- just convincing acting and knowledge of how humans think.

data.alt: The Fear, Greed, Urgency triangle that powers every scam
data.prompt: An equilateral triangle diagram on a blue (#2980B9) background. FEAR at top vertex, GREED at bottom-left, URGENCY at bottom-right. Center text reads Every Scam Lives Here. Each vertex shows example phrases. Educational flat style illustration.

data.content: You get a call: 'Sir, your Aadhaar has been linked to money laundering. A CBI officer will arrive at your home unless you cooperate NOW.' Your heart starts racing. That is **Fear** at work -- the most powerful of the three legs.
Fear shuts down your thinking brain. When you are panicking, you shift from 'let me think about this' to 'just make this stop.' That is exactly what the scammer wants. Panic is their best friend.

data.alt: A teen looking panicked at their phone while a scammer manipulates them with fear tactics
data.prompt: An Indian teen looking panicked at their phone screen showing a scary official-looking message. A shadowy figure behind the screen pulls puppet strings. Blue (#2980B9) color palette, flat educational illustration style.

data.question: What are the three psychological levers that power every scam?

options.text: Anger, Sadness, and Confusion
Fear, Greed, and Urgency
Trust, Hope, and Excitement
Boredom, Curiosity, and Loneliness

data.content: **Greed** works more quietly but is equally deadly. You get a Telegram DM: 'You have been selected for a special IPO allotment. Put in Rs 50,000 now to confirm your slot -- expected 3x returns in a month.' Nobody wants to miss out on easy money. The scammer is counting on that.

**Urgency** is the closer. It stops you from doing the one thing that would expose every scam: **pausing and thinking**. 'This offer expires in 15 minutes.' 'Your SIM will be deactivated in 2 hours.' 'The officer is already on his way.' That time pressure? It is always fake.

data.text: Yaar, think of it like this. Fear makes you panic, Greed makes you dream, and Urgency makes sure you do not stop to think. A scammer just needs two out of three -- and you are already in trouble.

data.question: A scammer uses the Fear lever. What does that do to your brain?

options.text: It makes you curious about the offer
It shifts you from logical thinking to panic mode
It makes you want to earn more money

data.definition: Voice phishing. Scamming someone over a phone call. The caller pretends to be from a trusted organization like a bank, TRAI, or police to steal money or information.

data.alt: Real scam script example showing how TRAI impersonation calls work
data.prompt: A phone screen showing a fake caller ID saying TRAI Official with a scam script in a speech bubble. Red warning indicators around it. Blue (#2980B9) background, flat educational illustration style.

data.content: The Pause Protocol: Next time something makes you feel fear plus urgency at the same time, STOP. Hang up. Do not click. Do not transfer. Give yourself 10 minutes and call the organization directly using the number on their official website -- never the number from the suspicious message.

data.definition: Sending fake emails, SMSes, or messages that look like they are from legitimate organizations to steal your login details, OTPs, or money.

data.question: What is 'vishing'?

options.text: Hacking someone's computer remotely
Scamming someone over a phone call by pretending to be from a trusted organization
Sending fake emails that look like bank messages

data.content: One more thing that throws people off: scammers often know your name, your bank, sometimes even the last 4 digits of your card. They buy this from data leaks -- leaked databases of hundreds of millions of Indians are sold online. This 'insider knowledge' makes them sound real. It is not proof of anything.
India's cybercrime helpline, 1930, received over 1.5 million calls in 2023. That is roughly one call every 20 seconds. You are not alone, and this is way more common than you think.

data.definition: A verification process where banks and financial companies confirm your identity using documents like Aadhaar, PAN, and address proof. Banks do require KYC updates occasionally, but they notify you through their official app or registered mail -- never through WhatsApp messages or random phone calls.

data.question: If a caller knows your name, bank, and the last 4 digits of your card, does that prove they are from your bank?

options.text: Yes, only your bank would know those details
No, this data is commonly available from data breaches and leaks
Maybe, you should share your OTP to verify

exercises.scenario: You get a WhatsApp message: 'Dear Customer, your SBI account has been suspended due to incomplete KYC. Click here to update within 24 hours to avoid permanent closure: bit.ly/sbi-kyc-update2024'
exercises.prompt: Which legs of the scam triangle are being used here? (Identify all that apply in your head, then pick the best answer)

options.text: Only Greed, they want you to click for an offer
Fear and Urgency, account suspension threat + 24-hour deadline
Only Fear, the account suspension threat
This is probably a real SBI message

exercises.explanation: Classic two-leg attack: Fear (account suspended, permanent closure) + Urgency (24 hours). Real banks send KYC notices via registered post and official app notifications, never WhatsApp with a short link. The 'bit.ly' link is a huge red flag; SBI's real domain is onlinesbi.sbi.

exercises.prompt: Sort these phrases into which scam leg they represent

exercises.explanation: Every phrase maps to a scam lever. Fear creates panic (shuts down thinking). Greed creates desire (overrides caution). Urgency prevents you from pausing to verify. When you see all three in a single message, run.

exercises.prompt: A scammer calls and says: 'I'm Officer Sharma from the Cyber Crime Department. Your phone number was used to send 2,847 illegal messages. I'm giving you one chance to cooperate before I file the FIR.' What's the FIRST thing you should do?

options.text: Cooperate and answer their questions to prove your innocence

exercises.explanation: Real police do NOT call to warn you before filing an FIR, they just file it. Real officers do NOT take payments over the phone. The moment someone creates this kind of 'cooperate or face consequences' scenario on a call, hang up. Then call 1930 to check if any actual complaint exists against your number.

exercises.prompt: If a scammer knows your name, bank name, and the last 4 digits of your card, it proves they're really from your bank.
exercises.explanation: This is one of scammers' most powerful tricks -- using leaked data to seem legitimate. Millions of Indians' data (names, phone numbers, partial card numbers) have been leaked from apps, hospitals, telcos, and e-commerce sites. A scammer buying this data can sound remarkably convincing. Real banks will NEVER use this information to 'verify' themselves -- it's supposed to be YOU proving your identity to THEM, not the other way.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are legitimate reasons a real bank or government body might contact you? (Select all that apply)

options.text: To remind you that your FD is maturing
To ask for your OTP so they can 'verify your account'
To tell you about a new loan or credit card offer
To tell you your account will be frozen unless you transfer money to a 'safe account'
To notify you that your account statement is ready

exercises.explanation: Banks legitimately call for FD reminders, product offers, and statement notifications. What they will NEVER do: ask for your OTP, PIN, CVV, or full card number. They will NEVER ask you to transfer money to a 'safe account' (no such thing exists, this is the most common fraud script in India right now).

lessons.title: UPI Scams
lessons.subtitle: QR Codes, Collect Requests & the OLX Trap

data.content: You are selling your old phone on OLX for Rs 12,000. A buyer messages you -- says he is an Army officer posted in Ladakh, cannot meet in person, but he is very interested. He offers full price, zero bargaining. 'I will transfer the advance right now. Just scan this QR code to receive the money.'

data.text: Okay, that already feels off. Who pays full price without even bargaining? And since when do you need to scan something to RECEIVE money? That is like being asked to open your wallet to get paid.

data.content: You scan the QR code. Your UPI app opens. You enter your PIN. And Rs 5,000 leaves your account. You did not receive anything -- you **sent** money. The 'buyer' has blocked you. Welcome to India's most common UPI scam.

data.definition: A method of paying via UPI by scanning a Quick Response code. Scanning always initiates a payment FROM you. You can never receive money by scanning a QR code.

data.content: Tattoo this on your brain: **Scanning a QR code can ONLY send money. You CANNOT receive money by scanning a QR code.** Ever. Period. If someone asks you to scan a QR to receive payment, that is a scam. No exceptions. Not on GPay, not on PhonePe, not on Paytm. Nowhere.

data.question: Can you receive money by scanning a QR code?

options.text: Yes, if the sender sets it up correctly
No, scanning a QR code can only send money, never receive it
Yes, but only on Google Pay

data.definition: A request sent through UPI that, if you approve it, pulls money FROM your account TO the requester. Think of it like a debit, not a credit.

data.alt: Two-direction diagram showing UPI send vs receive flow
data.prompt: Two side-by-side flow diagrams. Left shows Sending Money flow with PIN entry and money going out. Right shows Receiving Money flow where you do nothing and money comes in. Bold labels PIN equals Money Out and No PIN equals Money In. Blue (#2980B9) educational flat style.

data.content: Here is how UPI actually works. Two directions: **Send** (you initiate, you enter PIN, money goes OUT) and **Receive** (someone sends to your UPI ID, no PIN needed, money comes IN). You only ever enter your PIN when money is leaving. If someone asks you to enter your PIN to 'receive' money, stop right there.

data.alt: A fake collect request notification that tricks people into sending money
data.prompt: A phone screen showing a fake UPI collect request notification saying Approve to receive Rs 5000 with a red warning overlay showing this actually SENDS money. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration.

data.question: When you receive money via UPI, what do you need to do?

options.text: Enter your UPI PIN to accept the payment
Approve a collect request notification
Nothing at all -- the money arrives automatically

data.content: Now the sneakier version: **Collect Requests**. A scammer sends you a collect request through GPay or PhonePe. It looks like a payment notification. The message says 'Anil Kumar has sent you Rs 5,000. Approve to receive.' But approving does not receive money -- it **authorizes** them to pull Rs 5,000 from your account.

data.text: Simple rule, bhai. If I need to enter my PIN or approve something, money is leaving. If money is coming to me, I literally do nothing. No PIN, no approval, nothing. It just shows up in my account. That is it.

data.question: You get a notification: 'Approve to receive Rs 2,000 from Rahul.' You don't know any Rahul. What is really happening?

options.text: Someone named Rahul is trying to send you money
It is a collect request -- approving it will SEND Rs 2,000 FROM your account to the scammer
Your UPI app has a glitch, restart it and try again
It is safe to approve small amounts like Rs 2,000

data.definition: Scammer convinces you to install AnyDesk or TeamViewer under the guise of helping with KYC or bank issues. They then watch your screen, read your OTPs, and drain your account.

data.content: The AnyDesk scam is particularly nasty. Someone calls saying they are from Google Pay customer care (which does not even exist -- GPay has no phone support). They say your account has a problem and need to 'see your screen to fix it.' Once AnyDesk is installed, they see everything -- including OTPs popping up on your screen.

Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm do NOT have customer care phone numbers that call you. Their support is only through the app. Any number claiming to be 'UPI customer care' on Google Search is almost certainly a scam -- some are literally paid ads placed by fraudsters. Yes, scammers buy Google Ads.

data.question: Someone asks you to install AnyDesk to fix a 'Google Pay issue.' What should you do?

options.text: Install it -- they just want to help fix the problem
Refuse -- Google Pay has no phone support, and AnyDesk gives full screen access to scammers
Install it but watch your screen carefully

data.alt: A swapped QR code at a street food stall redirecting payments to a scammer
data.prompt: A street food stall scene where a scammer has pasted their own QR code over the shop original QR code. A customer scans it unknowingly. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration style.

data.content: Another growing scam: **fake merchant QR codes**. Someone sticks their own QR code on top of a chai stall's real QR. You scan what you think is the shop's code, but the money goes to a scammer. The shopkeeper does not know. Always check that the payee name on your UPI app matches the shop before entering your PIN.

data.question: Your UPI app shows a different payee name than the shop you are paying at. What should you do?

options.text: Pay anyway, business names can differ from registered names
Stop the payment and alert the shopkeeper -- the QR code may have been swapped by a scammer
Pay a small test amount first to see where it goes

data.content: Before every UPI payment: (1) Check the payee name -- does it match who you expect? (2) Check the amount -- is this what you agreed? (3) Check your balance after -- did it change correctly? 10 seconds of verification beats hours of trying to recover lost money.

The QR code is set to pull Rs 4,000 from your account, not send to you. The 'once I see you've received it' creates false legitimacy. Real buyers pay you first by entering your UPI ID, you don't need to do anything to receive money.

exercises.prompt: A UPI collect request arrives from an unknown number with the note 'Refund from Amazon.' You were expecting a refund. What should you do?

options.text: Approve it, it's probably your refund

A collect request from 'Amazon' is always a scam. The note 'Refund from Amazon' is bait designed to match something you're already expecting.

exercises.prompt: You can receive money through UPI without entering your PIN.
exercises.explanation: Yes, receiving money requires absolutely nothing from you. Someone enters your UPI ID, their PIN, and money arrives in your account. You never enter your PIN when receiving. If you're entering a PIN, money is leaving. This is the core logic that exposes every 'receive by scanning' scam.

exercises.explanation: Always match the UPI payee name to who you expect to pay. QR code swapping, where scammers replace merchant QR codes with their own, is a real and growing fraud method. If the name doesn't match, don't pay. Alert the shop owner, they may not know their QR was replaced.

lessons.title: OTP Fraud
lessons.subtitle: The Last Door -- And Why You Must Never Open It

data.content: Think of your bank account as a locker room with three doors. Your password is the first door. Your PIN is the second. But the final door -- the one that stands between a scammer and your money even if they have cracked everything else -- is your **OTP**.

data.alt: A bank vault with three doors representing password, PIN, and OTP layers of security
data.prompt: A bank vault with three sequential doors. First door labeled Password, second labeled PIN, third labeled OTP. The OTP door glows as the final barrier. Blue (#2980B9) color scheme, flat educational illustration.

data.definition: A temporary 6-digit code sent to your registered mobile number to verify you are who you say you are. Valid for 30 to 60 seconds only. The final security door before any transaction goes through.

data.content: OTP stands for One-Time Password. It is a 6-digit number that expires in 30 to 60 seconds, sent ONLY to your registered mobile. The entire point? Even if a scammer has your password and PIN, they still cannot get in because they do not have your physical phone.

data.question: What is the purpose of an OTP in banking?

options.text: It is a permanent password for your account
It is a temporary code to verify that you authorized a transaction
It is a code that the bank uses to contact you

data.text: So the OTP is literally the last wall between a scammer and your money? And people just... tell it to strangers on the phone?!

data.content: Never share your OTP. Not with your bank. Not with your mom. Not with anyone who calls claiming to be from Paytm. The person who needs your OTP the most is the person trying to rob you. Real systems send the OTP to verify YOU -- they never need you to read it out loud.

Here is a real script scammers use when they call pretending to be SBI or HDFC: 'Sir, we noticed an unauthorized login attempt on your account. To secure your account, I need to verify your identity. I am sending you an OTP -- please tell me what it says so I can block the suspicious access.'

Sounds helpful, right? Here is what is actually happening: the scammer triggered a transaction to steal your money, and that OTP is the authorization code for THAT transaction. You read it out, they type it in, and your money is gone.

data.question: A 'bank employee' calls and asks you to share your OTP to 'block a suspicious transaction.' What is actually happening?

options.text: They are protecting your account from fraud
The OTP they triggered is for a transaction they want to steal from you
They need the OTP to verify their own identity

data.alt: How a vishing call tricks you into sharing your OTP
data.prompt: Split screen illustration. Left side shows a scammer at a desk triggering a bank transaction. Right side shows a victim on the phone reading the OTP aloud. Arrows show money flowing from victim to scammer. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational style.

data.definition: A scammer visits your telecom store with fake documents and convinces them to port your mobile number to a new SIM. Once they have your number, they receive all your OTPs and can access your bank accounts.

data.content: SIM swap is more sophisticated. The scammer already has your name and address from leaked data. They walk into a Jio or Airtel store with a fake Aadhaar and say your old SIM was lost. Once they get your number on their SIM, all OTPs go to them.

The first sign of a SIM swap? Your phone suddenly loses network signal entirely -- not just weak bars, but zero bars in a place where you normally have full signal. If that happens out of nowhere, call your telecom operator immediately from another phone.

data.alt: Step by step diagram of how a SIM swap attack works
data.prompt: Four-step infographic showing SIM swap attack. Step 1: Scammer buys leaked data. Step 2: Visits telecom store with fake ID. Step 3: Victim phone loses signal. Step 4: Scammer receives OTPs and drains account. Blue (#2980B9) background, flat educational illustration.

data.question: Your phone suddenly loses network signal completely in an area where it normally works. What could this indicate?

options.text: Routine network maintenance by your telecom operator
A possible SIM swap attack -- someone may have ported your number to their SIM
Your phone battery is too low for signal

data.text: The scary part about SIM swap is that your phone just goes dead. No warning, no message. By the time you figure out what happened, they have already received your OTPs and emptied your account. Speed matters -- seconds, not hours.

data.definition: Malicious apps hidden on your phone that silently forward your incoming SMS messages, including OTPs, to scammers. Usually installed from suspicious links or unofficial app stores.

data.content: There is also **OTP forwarding malware** -- apps that hide in your phone and automatically forward all incoming SMSes (including OTPs) to scammers. This is why you should never install apps from outside the Play Store or App Store, especially ones sent via WhatsApp links like 'Install this modified GPay for extra cashback.'

data.question: Your friend sends you an APK file on WhatsApp: 'Bro install this modified PhonePe, it gives 5% extra cashback.' What should you do?

options.text: Install it -- your friend would not send something harmful
Do not install it -- apps from outside Play Store or App Store can contain OTP-forwarding malware
Install it but disable SMS permissions
Scan it with your phone's antivirus first, then install

data.content: Simple OTP hygiene: (1) Never share an OTP with anyone on a call. (2) Never type an OTP into a website you did not navigate to yourself. (3) If your phone loses signal suddenly, call your operator immediately from another phone. (4) Enable SIM lock or port protection -- most operators offer this for free.

RBI made it mandatory for banks to mention the transaction purpose in OTP messages. If your OTP SMS does not say what it is for -- what amount, to whom -- that is a red flag in itself. A good OTP message always tells you: what is happening, how much, and where.

exercises.scenario: You receive a call: 'Hello, I'm Priya from HDFC Bank. We've detected a suspicious Rs 49,000 transaction on your account from Bengaluru. To block this, I'm sending you an OTP. Please share it with me immediately so we can cancel the transaction.'
exercises.prompt: What's the correct response?

options.text: Share the OTP, you need to stop the Rs 49,000 transaction
Ask for her employee ID before sharing the OTP
Hang up, then call HDFC's official number (1800-202-6161) to check your account
Share only the first 3 digits of the OTP as a compromise

exercises.explanation: The Rs 49,000 suspicious transaction is bait -- it makes you feel like sharing the OTP will protect you. But the OTP they're asking for is actually for the Rs 49,000 transaction they're trying to initiate. Hang up. Log into your actual HDFC app or call their official number to check. Real fraud alerts are informational -- they don't need your OTP to 'block' a transaction.

exercises.prompt: If an OTP message says it's for a Rs 30,000 transfer that you didn't initiate, you should enter it into the site you're on to 'cancel' the transfer.
exercises.explanation: An OTP can only AUTHORIZE a transaction -- it cannot cancel one. If you see an OTP for a transaction you didn't start, it means someone else triggered it. Don't enter the OTP anywhere. Call your bank immediately to report unauthorized activity. Entering the OTP completes the transaction, the opposite of canceling it.

exercises.prompt: Your phone suddenly shows 'No Service' in an area where it normally works fine. It's been that way for 20 minutes. What should you do?

options.text: Wait, probably just a network issue
Restart your phone and wait another hour
Call your telecom operator immediately from another phone to check for unauthorized SIM activity
Visit the nearest tower location to check signal

exercises.explanation: Sudden unexplained signal loss is a key warning sign of a SIM swap attack. While you're wondering what's wrong with your phone, a scammer might have your number on their SIM and is receiving your OTPs. Call your operator (Jio: 199, Airtel: 121, Vi: 199) from a family member's phone immediately. Faster is better -- every minute matters.

exercises.prompt: Sort these situations -- should you share or not share your OTP?

items.text: Logging into your own bank app, OTP sent to verify it's you
A caller from 'SBI' asks for your OTP to 'secure' your account
Completing an online purchase on an official website, OTP to confirm payment
A WhatsApp message from 'Google Pay Support' asking for your OTP

exercises.explanation: The rule is simple: you only enter an OTP on a screen YOU navigated to, for a transaction YOU initiated. You never speak an OTP out loud to anyone. You never type it into a link someone sent you. The OTP box you're typing into should always be on an app or website you opened yourself.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are warning signs that a call asking for your OTP is fraudulent? (Select all that apply)

options.text: They called you, you didn't call them
They create urgency ('act now or account will be frozen')
They know your name and partial account details
They say sharing the OTP will 'protect' your account
They have a professional-sounding automated menu (press 1 for English, press 2 for Hindi) before connecting you to a 'representative'

exercises.explanation: All five are red flags. Scammers call YOU (banks only call for pre-scheduled callbacks or post-complaint follow-ups). They create urgency. They use leaked data to sound credible. They reframe OTP sharing as protective. And they use professional automated phone menus that sound just like a real bank's system -- you can literally buy a fake one for Rs 5,000 online. None of this indicates legitimacy.

lessons.title: Too Good to Be True
lessons.subtitle: Investment Scams, Ponzi Schemes & Fake Trading Apps

data.content: You get added to a WhatsApp group called 'Stock Market Millionaires.' A guy named 'Finance Guru Suresh Ji' posts a screenshot every morning: 'Today's trade: +Rs 28,000 in 2 hours using my secret algorithm.' Other members are cheering: 'Suresh Ji zindabad!' Sounds legit?

data.text: Rs 28,000 in 2 hours?! That is literally more than most adults earn in a month. How can anyone believe that?

data.content: People believe it because the scam validates itself first. In 2018, a man named Amit Bhardwaj promised his audience something wild: invest your Bitcoin with him, and he would return 10 Bitcoin per month for every 10 invested. 100% monthly returns. He collected Rs 2,000 to 8,000 crore before it all collapsed. His scheme was called GainBitcoin.

data.definition: A fake investment where returns to existing investors are paid using money from new investors, not from real profits. Works until new investors dry up, then collapses completely. Named after Charles Ponzi, who ran one in 1920.

data.content: In 2010-2011, Speak Asia Online promised Rs 11,000 per month to anyone who paid Rs 11,000 to join and filled out online 'surveys.' About 2 million Indians signed up. The surveys were fake. The money came from new joiners. Classic Ponzi. When new members dried up, it collapsed, and everyone's money vanished.

data.alt: How a Ponzi scheme grows and eventually collapses
data.prompt: An upside-down funnel or pyramid diagram. Top shows founder taking money. Middle layers show waves of investors with money flowing upward to pay earlier investors. Bottom shows collapse when new investors stop. Timeline graph on the side rises then crashes. Blue (#2980B9) educational flat style.

data.question: In a Ponzi scheme, where do the 'returns' paid to early investors come from?

options.text: From real profits generated by the investment
From money put in by newer investors
From a government subsidy fund

data.content: India's best legitimate investment -- the Nifty 50 index -- has returned about 12 to 14% annually over 20 years. If someone promises you 30% monthly, that is 360% annually. Where is this magic money tree? Can I also visit it?

Here is the thing about Ponzi schemes: they feel real for a while. Early investors actually receive their 'returns.' Word spreads. Your uncle made money. Your neighbor made money. So you put money in. This is exactly how smart people get trapped -- the scheme validates itself until it suddenly does not.

data.alt: A WhatsApp trading group full of fake profit screenshots and bot accounts
data.prompt: A phone screen showing a WhatsApp group chat with fake profit screenshots, bot members cheering, and a group admin posting Trade of the Day. Red flags highlighted around the screen. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration.

data.content: Today's version runs through **Telegram groups** and **Instagram DMs**. You get added to a group with a 'mentor' posting daily profit screenshots. Members (actually fake accounts or bots) cheer and post their own 'wins.' Then comes the hook: join the premium group for Rs 5,000. Once you pay, poof -- 'Suresh Ji' was never real.

data.question: India's Nifty 50 index has returned about 12-14% annually over 20 years. Someone promises you 30% monthly returns. Is this realistic?

options.text: Yes, if they have a special algorithm
No, 30% monthly is 360% annually -- far beyond what any legitimate investment can deliver
Maybe, crypto can deliver those kinds of returns

data.definition: Scammers heavily promote a penny stock or crypto coin to drive up the price, then sell their own holdings at the peak, leaving everyone else with worthless assets.

data.term: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India)
data.definition: The regulatory body that oversees all stock market activity in India. Anyone giving investment advice for money must be registered with SEBI. Check registration at sebi.gov.in before investing.

data.text: Easiest test in the world, bhai. Can you verify the company or advisor on SEBI's website? Go to sebi.gov.in, search their name. If they are not registered, do not give them a single rupee. Takes two minutes. Literally two minutes.

data.question: How can you verify if an investment advisor or platform is legitimate in India?

options.text: Check if they have a professional website and good reviews
Check their SEBI registration at sebi.gov.in
Ask them for a money-back guarantee
See if your friends have invested with them

data.content: **Fake trading apps** are the newest evolution. You get recruited on Instagram or Telegram to a platform that looks like a real broker -- slick UI, live charts, portfolio tracking. You 'invest' Rs 10,000. You watch it grow to Rs 50,000 on screen. You try to withdraw. Suddenly there are 'taxes,' 'compliance fees,' 'withdrawal processing charges.' Every fee you pay disappears. The Rs 50,000 was never real.

data.alt: A fake trading app showing fake profits with withdrawal fees that never end
data.prompt: A phone showing a professional-looking trading app with fake profits displayed. A pop-up says Pay Rs 8000 withdrawal fee. Behind the phone, the profits are shown as smoke or illusion dissolving. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration.

data.question: You invested Rs 10,000 on a trading app and it shows Rs 50,000 profit. When you try to withdraw, they ask for Rs 8,000 in 'processing fees.' What is happening?

options.text: Normal withdrawal fees -- pay and collect your Rs 50,000
The Rs 50,000 was never real -- it is a fake app designed to extract more money from you through endless fees
Ask for a receipt of the fees, then it is safe to pay
Pay the fee since you will still profit Rs 32,000 after all deductions

data.content: You can literally buy a fake trading app interface online for a few thousand rupees. The charts move, the portfolio updates, profits look real. But there is zero connection to any actual stock exchange. It is pure theatre designed to take your money.

If you have already lost money to an investment scam, you might be targeted AGAIN by 'recovery agents' who claim they can get your money back for an upfront fee. They cannot. This is a secondary scam targeting people who have already been victimized. The only legitimate recovery path is through police and cybercrime.gov.in.

exercises.scenario: A cousin adds you to a WhatsApp group called 'Wealth Builders India.' The admin, 'Finance Guru Suresh Ji,' posts screenshots every day showing profits: 'Today's trade: +Rs 28,000 in 2 hours using my secret algorithm.' Other members post 'Thank you Suresh Ji! Changed my life!' He invites you to invest a minimum Rs 25,000 to join his 'premium strategy.' He's been doing this for 8 months and your cousin says he's 'legit.'
exercises.prompt: Which red flags are present in this scenario? (Choose the best answer)

options.text: None, if your cousin vouches for him and he's been running for 8 months, it's probably legitimate
Multiple red flags: unverifiable screenshots, social proof from unknown accounts, no SEBI mention, WhatsApp recruitment, minimum investment pressure
One red flag, the screenshots could be fake. Everything else seems okay.
The only concern is the Rs 25,000 minimum, if you invest less, the risk is lower

exercises.explanation: This is a textbook Telegram/WhatsApp investment fraud. Daily screenshots of profits are trivially easy to fake. 'Members' are often bot accounts or paid participants. 8 months of operation proves nothing -- Speak Asia ran for years before collapsing. Your cousin being in it doesn't validate it; they might already be a victim who's hoping to earn referral commissions. Check SEBI first. If Suresh Ji isn't registered, it's over.

exercises.prompt: An app promises '3% daily returns on crypto investments, verified by 50,000 users.' You invest Rs 20,000 and the app shows your balance growing to Rs 1,10,000 in 40 days. When you try to withdraw, they say you owe Rs 8,000 in 'GST and processing fees.' What's happening?

options.text: Legitimate, withdrawal fees are normal in crypto platforms
Fake trading app scam, the Rs 1,10,000 was never real; the fees will also disappear
Pay the fee, you'll still profit Rs 82,000 after all
Ask for a receipt of the fees as proof before paying

exercises.explanation: 3% daily = ~90% monthly = ~2,700% annually. Physically impossible from real markets. The growing balance was fake -- just numbers on a screen. When they ask for 'fees before withdrawal,' those fees will also vanish. Then there will be more fees. This pattern is called an 'advance fee scam' layered on top of a fake trading platform. No legitimate platform requires you to pay in order to receive your own money.

exercises.prompt: SEBI-registered investment advisors are allowed to guarantee returns on their recommendations.
exercises.explanation: SEBI explicitly prohibits registered advisors from guaranteeing returns. The stock market has risk by nature -- anyone guaranteeing returns is either lying or operating illegally. This is one of the fastest ways to spot a fraud: if they guarantee returns, they're not legitimate, regardless of how professional they look.

exercises.prompt: Sort these into Legitimate Investment Behavior or Investment Scam Red Flag

items.text: SEBI registration number displayed prominently
'Guaranteed 5% monthly returns, no risk'
Mutual fund that mentions past performance doesn't guarantee future returns
Must recruit 3 friends to unlock higher returns
Investment involves market risk and may go down
Pay Rs 2,000 fee to withdraw your own profits

exercises.explanation: Legitimate investments are transparent about risk, show proper regulatory credentials, and never require recruitment of others for returns. If an 'investment' sounds like a job where you earn by recruiting, it's MLM or Ponzi territory. Real investing is boring. It should feel boring.

exercises.prompt: Which of these would be red flags in a chit fund or investment scheme? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Monthly meetings where cash is pooled and bid upon
No written agreement or receipt given for your investment
Returns dependent on how many new members join
The scheme is not registered with RBI or SEBI
Promoter is not contactable once you've paid

exercises.explanation: Traditional registered chit funds (covered under the Chit Funds Act) are legitimate -- members pool money, bid for the pot, and the organizer is registered. Red flags: no receipts, returns tied to recruitment, unregistered operation, and disappearing promoters. Real chit fund organizers are registered with State Governments and issue formal receipts.

lessons.title: Protecting Your Parents & Grandparents
lessons.subtitle: Because Scammers Know Who to Target

data.content: Your grandmother gets a phone call. A serious, official-sounding voice says: 'Namaskar, I am calling from the Aadhaar Seva Kendra. Your Aadhaar card is about to be permanently suspended. Your bank accounts linked to this Aadhaar will also be frozen. Please provide your Aadhaar number, bank details, and the OTP we are sending to your mobile.'

data.text: This is scary because Nani would totally believe this. She has no clue that UIDAI never calls people. And if she is home alone during the day, there is nobody around to tell her it is a scam.

data.content: She is 68. She does not know that Aadhaar cannot be 'suspended for not updating.' She is scared. She cooperates. By the time the family finds out, Rs 1.8 lakh has been transferred out. This story happens thousands of times a week across India.

Scammers target older adults deliberately -- not because elders are dumb, but because they may be less familiar with digital systems, more trusting of authority figures, and often home alone during the day when nobody can intervene. This is a calculated tactic, not a character flaw.

data.question: Why do scammers specifically target older adults?

options.text: Because older adults have more money than young people
Because they may be less familiar with digital systems, more trusting of authority, and often home alone during the day
Because older adults cannot use smartphones

data.alt: Common scams targeting elders in India with their red flags
data.prompt: A four-panel grid showing common elder-targeting scams. Panel 1: Aadhaar Suspension call. Panel 2: KYC Expiry call. Panel 3: Fake CBI call. Panel 4: Lottery prize call. Each panel has the scam script in red and the truth in green. Blue (#2980B9) borders, flat educational style.

data.content: **The Aadhaar Suspension Call:** 'Your Aadhaar will be blocked. Provide your number, bank details, and OTP.' The truth? UIDAI does not call citizens. Aadhaar cannot be suspended for non-use. The UIDAI helpline is 1947 -- that is how you call THEM, not how they call you.

data.definition: A scam where fraudsters impersonate police, CBI, ED, or customs officers and keep victims on a phone or video call for hours or days, creating the illusion of an investigation while demanding money to settle a fake case.

data.content: **The Fake CBI/Police Call** is even more terrifying. 'A criminal case has been filed against your family member for money laundering. Pay to settle this quietly and avoid arrest.' This is called **digital arrest** -- keeping someone in prolonged fear over a phone call. In 2024, Indians lost over Rs 2,140 crore to digital arrest scams alone.

data.question: What is a 'digital arrest' scam?

options.text: When police arrest someone online through a warrant
When scammers impersonate police or CBI and keep victims on a call for hours, demanding money to settle a fake case
When your phone is locked remotely by hackers

data.alt: Digital arrest scam showing a victim trapped on a video call with a fake officer
data.prompt: An elderly person sitting scared in front of a laptop showing a video call with someone in a fake police uniform. The room feels like a trap. A clock on the wall shows hours passing. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration.

data.definition: A payment system that uses your Aadhaar number and fingerprint to withdraw or transact from your bank account -- no card or phone needed. Useful in rural India but vulnerable to fingerprint cloning.

data.content: **The AePS Biometric Scam** is growing fast in rural India. Scammers clone fingerprint data -- sometimes from biometric logs of MGNREGA work or government enrollment -- and use silicone fingerprints to authenticate Aadhaar-enabled withdrawals. States like Jharkhand and Bihar have seen the most cases.

The fix is simple: lock your Aadhaar biometrics via myAadhaar.uidai.gov.in or the mAadhaar app. When locked, nobody can use your fingerprint for any AePS transaction. Unlock only when you actually need it, then lock again.

data.question: How can you protect yourself from AePS biometric fraud?

options.text: Avoid giving your fingerprint anywhere, including government offices
Lock your Aadhaar biometrics at myAadhaar.uidai.gov.in or the mAadhaar app, and unlock only when needed
AePS fraud cannot be prevented, it is a government system flaw
Change your Aadhaar number every year

data.text: The key is giving your family practical tools, not lectures. Nobody wants to be told they are gullible. Set up a family code word. Register DND. Lock their Aadhaar biometrics. These are things you can do in one Sunday afternoon.

data.content: The Family Code Word System: Agree on a secret word or phrase with your parents and grandparents that only your family knows. If anyone calls claiming to be a family member in trouble ('Your grandson has been arrested, send money now'), they must use the code word to verify. Scammers cannot know your word.

data.question: What is the Family Code Word System and why is it useful?

options.text: A password for the family Wi-Fi network
A secret word only your family knows, used to verify identity during emergency calls -- it defeats voice cloning scams
A code you share with your bank for extra security

data.alt: A family setting up protective measures together on their phones
data.prompt: An Indian family scene with a teenager helping grandparents set up Aadhaar biometric lock and DND on their phones. Warm supportive atmosphere. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration style.

data.definition: A TRAI service activated by calling 1909. It blocks unsolicited marketing and spam calls and SMSes to your number, reducing the chance of scam calls reaching your phone.

data.content: Practical things to set up with your elders this weekend: (1) Add DND to their number via 1909 to reduce scam calls. (2) Show them how to hang up and call you first when any 'authority' calls asking for money or info. (3) Lock their Aadhaar biometrics. (4) Add transaction alerts on their bank accounts so you get notified of any unusual activity.

AI voice cloning can now replicate a person's voice from just a few seconds of audio -- like a birthday video on the family WhatsApp group. Scammers use cloned voices to impersonate family members in 'emergency' calls. A code word system defeats this completely, because no AI can guess your family's secret word.

exercises.scenario: Your 70-year-old grandfather calls you, very stressed: 'A man from UIDAI called and said my Aadhaar will be cancelled tomorrow. He needs my Aadhaar number and the OTP he's going to send to confirm my identity. He sounds very official. Should I give it?'
exercises.prompt: What do you tell your grandfather?

options.text: Tell him to give only the Aadhaar number, not the OTP, to be safe
Tell him UIDAI does not call citizens, this is a scam, and to hang up immediately
Tell him to ask the caller for his employee ID and call UIDAI to verify
Tell him to give the OTP only if they can prove they're from UIDAI first

exercises.explanation: UIDAI (the Aadhaar authority) does NOT call citizens. Aadhaar cannot be 'cancelled for not updating.' The caller knows your grandfather's number because it was bought from leaked data -- that's all they know. Telling your grandfather to hang up is the correct response. Then reassure him: his Aadhaar is fine. The UIDAI helpline is 1947 if you want to double-check, but he should CALL them, not receive calls FROM them.

exercises.scenario: Your mother receives a call from someone claiming to be a 'CBI officer.' He says your father's company account has been linked to a money laundering case. He insists your mother stay on the video call and not speak to anyone -- 'this is a government investigation, you cannot inform others.' He's been on the call for 3 hours. Your mother texts you secretly: 'Someone from CBI is investigating Papa. I'm scared.'
exercises.prompt: What's the correct response?

options.text: Tell her to cooperate, a 3-hour government investigation sounds serious
Tell her this is 'digital arrest' fraud, hang up immediately, you'll call back in 2 minutes
Ask her to get the officer's badge number before hanging up
Call your father's company first to check if there's really a case

exercises.explanation: This is the 'digital arrest' scam -- keeping victims isolated on a call for hours, creating psychological pressure to pay. The 'don't inform others' instruction is designed to prevent exactly what your mother did (texting you). Real government investigations involve written notices, in-person visits, and legal processes -- never 3-hour video calls demanding silence. Tell her to hang up NOW. The call is the crime.

exercises.prompt: Sort these elder-protection actions -- should you do them or skip them?

items.text: Register parents' number on DND via 1909
Shame them if they fall for a scam so they're more careful next time
Set up transaction SMS alerts on their bank account
Lock Aadhaar biometrics on myAadhaar.uidai.gov.in
Tell them to cooperate with any caller who sounds official
Create a family code word to verify real emergencies

exercises.explanation: Practical protection beats lectures. DND reduces contact with scammers. Transaction alerts give you early warning. Aadhaar biometric lock prevents AePS fraud. A code word system defuses the 'grandchild in trouble' scam. And shame after a scam only makes recovery harder -- understanding and action is what helps.

exercises.prompt: Your grandmother says 'They told me I've won Rs 12 lakh in an SBI lucky draw but I need to pay Rs 3,000 to release the prize money.' What's true?

options.text: SBI does run lucky draws, she should pay the fee and claim her prize
Pay only Rs 500 as a token amount to test if it's real
There is no SBI lucky draw, legitimate prizes never require an upfront fee to claim
Ask SBI's official branch to verify before paying the fee

exercises.explanation: SBI does not run 'lucky draws' where random winners are called. This is a classic advance fee fraud -- the Rs 3,000 'processing fee' will vanish, and then there will be more fees (GST, tax, insurance, etc.) until the victim stops paying. The prize never arrives. No legitimate lottery or prize ever requires you to pay money to collect your winnings -- that's illegal in India.

exercises.prompt: Locking your Aadhaar biometrics on the UIDAI website means you can never use your fingerprint for Aadhaar verification again, even for legitimate purposes.
exercises.explanation: Aadhaar biometric lock is temporary and reversible. You can unlock it anytime via myAadhaar.uidai.gov.in or the mAadhaar app using an OTP to your registered mobile. When locked, nobody -- including scammers with cloned fingerprints -- can use your biometric for AePS withdrawals. Unlock only when you need to use it, then lock again. This is especially important for elders whose fingerprint data may have been captured during MGNREGA or other government scheme enrollment.

data.content: First: breathe. This is not the end. Every year, Indian authorities recover hundreds of crores of scammed money -- because victims acted fast. The key word here? Fast. The faster you move in the next 30 minutes, the better your chances of getting your money back.

data.text: Think of it like this: the money you lost is sitting in the scammer's account right now. But it will not stay there long. They move it fast -- break it into small transfers, pull it out at ATMs, route it through 5 different accounts. Your job is to freeze that account before they empty it.

data.content: Second: it is NOT your fault. These scammers are professionals who run scripts tested on millions of people. They know exactly what to say and when to say it. You are not the first person they have fooled and you will not be the last. What matters now is what you do in the next 30 minutes.

Time is literally money right now. Every minute you spend feeling bad is a minute the scammer spends moving your cash further away. Freeze the transaction first, report second, feel the feelings third. You have permission to fall apart AFTER you make those calls.

data.definition: A written document prepared by police when they receive information about a crime. Filing an FIR is your legal right and is mandatory for the police to register for amounts above Rs 1 lakh. It strengthens your fraud recovery case.

data.alt: Emergency 30-minute action flowchart for fraud victims
data.prompt: A vertical 5-step emergency flowchart with clock icons. Step 1 (0-5 min): Call Bank. Step 2 (5-15 min): Call 1930. Step 3 (15-30 min): File at cybercrime.gov.in. Step 4 (Day 1-3): File FIR. Step 5 (Ongoing): Track status. Blue (#2980B9) background, flat educational illustration.

data.definition: A bank-initiated reversal of a transaction that was fraudulent. Success depends on how quickly you report it. The money must still be in the destination account for reversal to work. Faster means better chances.

data.content: **Step 1 (0 to 5 minutes): Call your bank's fraud helpline immediately.** Major bank numbers: SBI 1800-111-109, HDFC 1800-202-6161, ICICI 1800-1080, Axis 1800-419-5959, Kotak 1860-266-0811. Tell them: 'I have been a victim of fraud, I need to freeze my account and raise a chargeback.' Get a complaint ticket number.

data.question: After being scammed, what is the very first thing you should do?

options.text: Post about it on social media to warn others
Call your bank's fraud helpline to freeze your account and raise a chargeback
Wait 24 hours to see if the money comes back automatically

data.definition: India's 24/7 helpline for reporting financial cyber fraud. Operates under the Ministry of Home Affairs. Can coordinate with multiple banks to freeze scammer accounts. Always call this along with your bank.

data.content: **Step 2 (5 to 15 minutes): Call 1930.** This is the National Cyber Crime Helpline, available 24/7. Give them: your name, the scammer's phone number or UPI ID or bank account, the amount lost, and roughly when it happened. They can coordinate with banks across India to freeze the destination account before the money is withdrawn.

data.question: What is the 1930 helpline for?

options.text: General police complaints
India's 24/7 National Cyber Crime Helpline that can coordinate with banks to freeze scammer accounts
A toll-free banking customer support number

data.alt: The cybercrime.gov.in portal showing how to file a financial fraud complaint
data.prompt: A laptop screen showing the cybercrime.gov.in website with the Report Cyber Crime button highlighted and the Financial Fraud option selected. Arrows point to key fields to fill. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration.

data.text: So the order is: bank first to freeze, then 1930 to coordinate across banks, then cybercrime.gov.in for the official record. All within 30 minutes. Okay, I am writing this down.

data.content: **Step 3 (15 to 30 minutes): File at cybercrime.gov.in.** Click 'Report Cyber Crime,' select 'Financial Fraud.' You will need: the scammer's contact details, the transaction ID from your bank app, date and time of fraud, and your account details. This generates an official complaint number for tracking.

data.question: After being scammed, a 'recovery agent' online offers to get your money back for an upfront fee. Is this legitimate?

options.text: Yes, ethical hackers can trace and reverse transactions
No, this is a secondary scam targeting people who have already been victimized
Maybe, if they provide references from past clients

data.content: What to screenshot RIGHT NOW if you have been scammed: (1) The fraudster's phone number. (2) Any WhatsApp or SMS conversation. (3) The UPI transaction ID from your bank app. (4) Any QR codes or links they sent. (5) The scammer's UPI ID or bank account number. This is your evidence. Do not delete anything.

data.alt: A phone screen showing evidence that should be saved after a fraud
data.prompt: A phone screen with multiple screenshots arranged showing a scammer phone number, chat messages, UPI transaction ID, and a QR code. A Save Evidence label at the top. Blue (#2980B9) palette, flat educational illustration.

data.content: **What are the real chances of recovery?** Honest answer: it depends on speed. UPI frauds reported within the first hour have the best recovery rates because funds can still be in transit. Investment scam money is harder to recover since it gets broken into small transfers quickly. But even partial recovery is possible, and your reports help catch repeat scammers.

data.question: You reported a UPI fraud to your bank within 5 minutes and also called 1930 within 15 minutes. Why does this speed matter?

options.text: It does not matter -- recovery takes the same time regardless
Because the scammer's account can be frozen before they withdraw your money, maximizing recovery chances
Because banks only accept fraud complaints within the first hour
Because 1930 charges less if you call sooner

data.content: In 2023-24, the Ministry of Home Affairs reported that swift action via 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in helped freeze fraudulent funds worth Rs 1,127 crore. That is real money that went back to real victims. Reporting works. Always report.

exercises.prompt: Put these fraud-response steps in the correct order (fastest to slowest urgency)

items.text: Call 1930 National Cyber Crime Helpline
Call your bank's fraud helpline to freeze account
File an FIR at the local police station
File complaint on cybercrime.gov.in
Send a written complaint to RBI Banking Ombudsman (if bank doesn't cooperate)
Screenshot all scammer conversations and transaction IDs

exercises.explanation: Speed is the critical variable. Bank freeze + 1930 call + cybercrime.gov.in filing should all happen within the first 15-30 minutes, while the fraudulent money might still be in transit or in the destination account. FIR on the same day. Ombudsman escalation only if the bank refuses to cooperate, which has a 30-day legal deadline from the incident.

exercises.prompt: You were scammed Rs 40,000 via UPI 3 hours ago. You've already called your bank. What should you do next?

options.text: Wait to see if the bank reverses it automatically
Call 1930 and file on cybercrime.gov.in with the scammer's UPI ID and transaction ID
Contact the scammer again and try to negotiate the money back
Post about it on social media to warn others first

exercises.explanation: After calling your bank, 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in are the next stops. The scammer's UPI ID (visible in your transaction history) and the transaction reference number are the key pieces of evidence. 3 hours is still early enough for a potential freeze -- the median time for a successful freeze is within 6-8 hours of the fraud. Social media can come later; reporting first maximizes recovery chances.

exercises.scenario: After being scammed, your father searches Google for 'cyber fraud money recovery service' and finds a company that says: 'We recover scammed money using our network of ethical hackers. 90% success rate. Pay Rs 3,000 upfront and we'll return Rs 40,000 within 7 days.' He's considering paying.
exercises.prompt: What's this 'recovery service'?

options.text: Probably legitimate, 90% success rate sounds credible
A secondary scam targeting fraud victims, pay Rs 3,000 and lose that too
Worth trying as a last resort if police don't help
Ask them for references from previous clients first

exercises.explanation: This is one of the cruelest scams -- targeting people at their most vulnerable, immediately after they've already lost money. No private 'ethical hacker' can recover scammed money. Recovery only happens through official channels (bank freezes, police, NPCI). These 'recovery services' take your upfront fee and disappear. If references are provided, they're fake. The only path is 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in.

exercises.prompt: Which of these should you screenshot and save immediately after discovering you've been scammed? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The scammer's phone number from your call log
Any WhatsApp or SMS conversation with the scammer
The UPI transaction ID from your bank app
The scammer's UPI ID shown in your transaction history
Any links or QR codes they sent

exercises.explanation: All five are critical evidence. The scammer's number, conversation logs, transaction IDs, their UPI ID, and any links/QR codes they shared all help build the complaint and assist authorities in tracing the fraud. Don't delete any messages or call logs -- they're evidence. The more documentation you have, the stronger your case on cybercrime.gov.in and with police.

exercises.prompt: If you're a victim of UPI fraud, reporting it on the UPI app itself (PhonePe/Google Pay) does nothing useful.
exercises.explanation: Reporting fraud within your UPI app sends the complaint directly to NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India), which can flag and freeze the scammer's UPI ID across all UPI-linked apps simultaneously -- not just yours. This is actually one of the fastest ways to escalate UPI-specific fraud, and it works alongside (not instead of) calling 1930 and filing on cybercrime.gov.in.
