choices.feedback: This was actually legitimate. The sender is 'SBI-ALERTS' (official), there is no suspicious link, and 1800-111-109 is SBI's real number. Suspicious SMSes usually have short links and urgent language pressuring you to act.

display.message: Hi! I saw your listing on OLX for the guitar. I'm interested. I'm posted in Kargil with the Army and can't come pick up but I'll pay Rs 8,000 via UPI advance. Please share your UPI ID or scan my QR code to receive the money.

nodes.prompt: You are selling a guitar on OLX for Rs 8,500. What do you do?

choices.text: Share your UPI ID, receiving money requires no other action
choices.feedback: Smart. Sharing your UPI ID is safe -- the sender enters your ID and their own PIN. You do nothing. Money arrives. If they insist you need to 'scan to receive', that is when you know it is a scam.

choices.text: Scan the QR code they're offering to receive the advance
choices.feedback: You scanned the QR. Rs 5,000 just left your account. The 'Army officer' has vanished. Scanning a QR code sends money -- it cannot receive it. This is the most common OLX scam in India.

choices.text: Ignore completely, Army officer story sounds suspicious
choices.feedback: Cautious, but you could have handled it better. The Army story IS suspicious (it is a common script), but you could share your UPI ID safely and verify the payment arrived before doing anything else.

nodes.narrative: Your UPI app shows 'Payment of Rs 5,000 to Prashant K. successful.' Your phone rings -- it's a friend calling about lunch plans. You stare at the transaction. The 'buyer' has blocked you on WhatsApp.

choices.text: Report the fraud, call 1930 and flag the UPI ID
choices.feedback: Good recovery instinct. Report it, then continue.

choices.text: Ignore it and hope the money comes back on its own
choices.feedback: Ignoring fraud gives the scammer time to withdraw your money. Every minute you wait reduces recovery chances. Always report immediately to 1930 and your bank.

display.scenario: You pick up. A professional-sounding woman says: 'Hello, I'm calling from HDFC Bank's fraud prevention team. We've detected a suspicious login on your account from Pune. To secure your account, I'm sending you an OTP. Please share it with me immediately so I can block this access.'

nodes.prompt: The OTP arrives on your phone while she's speaking. What do you do?

choices.text: Hang up immediately, HDFC never asks for OTPs on calls
choices.feedback: Perfect. Banks NEVER ask for your OTP over a call. The OTP she triggered is for a transaction she is trying to initiate. Hanging up is exactly right. Call HDFC directly at 1800-202-6161 to verify your account is safe.

choices.text: Share the OTP, you need to stop the suspicious login
choices.feedback: You shared the OTP. A transaction for Rs 18,500 was just authorized from your account. The OTP she asked for was for THIS transaction -- she triggered it herself. Banks never need your OTP to 'protect' your account.

choices.text: Ask for her employee ID before sharing
choices.feedback: Asking for employee ID seems smart, but she will have one ready -- she can make up any 8-digit number. The question is never 'is this person who they say they are?' The question is: 'Does a bank EVER need my OTP over a call?' Answer: No. Hang up.

nodes.narrative: Your phone pings. HDFC SMS: 'Your account has been debited Rs 18,500 for online transaction. If not done by you, call 1800-202-6161.' The caller has already hung up.

choices.text: Call 1800-202-6161 immediately to freeze and file fraud complaint
choices.feedback: Good. Every second matters now. Continue.

choices.text: Try calling the scammer back to demand your money
choices.feedback: Calling the scammer back is pointless and dangerous -- they may try to extract more money or information from you. The number is likely a burner phone. Report to your bank and 1930 instead.

nodes.narrative: She gives you a convincing 8-digit ID: 'EMP-47821.' You share the OTP. Your account is debited Rs 18,500. Employee IDs can be faked in 3 seconds.

choices.text: Call HDFC's real helpline to freeze and report
choices.feedback: Good recovery. But remember: the question is never 'is this person real?' It is 'does a bank ever need my OTP over a call?' They do not.

choices.text: Search Google for 'HDFC fraud recovery service' and pay for help
choices.feedback: Online 'fraud recovery services' are themselves scams targeting people who have already been victimized. The only legitimate path is your bank's official helpline and the 1930 cybercrime helpline.

display.subject: Your Amazon Order Refund, Rs 1,299
display.message: Dear Customer, we are processing a refund of Rs 1,299 for order #408-XXXXX. To complete the refund, please verify your UPI ID by approving the collect request we have sent. This approval is required within 2 hours.

nodes.prompt: You do have a recent Amazon return pending. What do you do?

choices.text: Delete, fake email. Amazon refunds go directly to your account, no approval needed
choices.feedback: Excellent catch. Three red flags: (1) Domain is 'amazon-india-support.co.in', not amazon.in. (2) Amazon NEVER sends collect requests. (3) 2-hour urgency is a pressure tactic. Real refunds credit automatically -- you approve nothing.

choices.text: Approve the collect request, you're expecting this refund
choices.feedback: You approved the collect request. Rs 1,299 left your account, not arrived. The fake email used your actual pending refund (bought from data leaks or guessed) to make this seem legitimate. Always verify the sender domain before acting.

choices.text: Call Amazon customer care to verify
choices.feedback: Smart -- verifying is always right. When you call, they will confirm refunds credit automatically and no approval is required. The email is fake.

nodes.narrative: 'Payment of Rs 1,299 successful' -- outgoing. The refund never arrives. The email domain was a fake. Your actual Amazon refund will arrive in 3-5 days automatically. Nothing you needed to do.

choices.text: Note: approve no collect requests from strangers. Move on.
choices.feedback: Lesson learned. Moving on.

choices.text: Reply to the fake Amazon email asking them to reverse the transaction
choices.feedback: Replying to a scam email confirms your email is active and may lead to more phishing attempts. The email was not from Amazon. Never engage with the scammer -- report through official channels.

display.notification: Collect Request: Arjun has requested Rs 450 from you (Split: Dinner at Social, your share)
display.context: You went to dinner with your friends Arjun, Priya, and Karan last night. Total bill was Rs 1,800.

nodes.prompt: What do you do with this collect request?

choices.text: Approve it, Rs 450 is exactly your share of Rs 1,800 split 4 ways
choices.feedback: Correct. This is a legitimate collect request from someone you know, for an amount that matches a known event (last night's dinner, Rs 1,800 divided by 4 = Rs 450). Arjun's name, the context, and the amount all check out.

choices.text: Reject it, never approve collect requests
choices.feedback: You rejected a legitimate request from your friend. Collect requests from known contacts for verified amounts are fine to approve. The rule is not 'never approve collect requests' -- it is 'never approve from strangers or unknown sources.'

choices.text: Call Arjun to confirm before approving
choices.feedback: Also correct! Verifying with a quick call before approving is always safe. Arjun will confirm, you approve. Extra cautious, totally fine.

display.scenario: A panicked voice: 'Beta, yeh meri nani hai. Mere phone mein problem aa gayi. Main temporarily ek doosre number se bol rahi hoon. Mujhe abhi turant Rs 15,000 chahiye, medical emergency hai. Baad mein sab explain karuungi.' (It sounds exactly like your grandmother's voice.)

nodes.prompt: You haven't spoken to your grandmother recently. She does have some health issues.

choices.text: Transfer Rs 15,000, it sounds urgent and it's Nani's voice
choices.feedback: AI voice cloning can replicate a person's voice from social media clips. The 'new number due to phone problem' story prevents you from calling back to verify. This is an increasingly common scam -- always verify through a second channel.

choices.text: Use your family code word to verify, or call Nani's original number
choices.feedback: Perfect response. Call her original number to verify -- if she is actually in an emergency, she will answer or someone will. If the caller cannot provide your family code word, it is a scam. Voice cloning is real and growing.

choices.text: Tell the caller to contact another family member instead
choices.feedback: Smart redirect -- buying time to verify is the right instinct. Meanwhile, call Nani's actual number immediately to check.

nodes.narrative: You transfer Rs 15,000. An hour later, you call your grandmother's real number to check on her. She is absolutely fine, never called you, phone is working perfectly. Her voice was cloned from her birthday video on the family WhatsApp.

choices.text: Report to 1930 immediately and call your bank
choices.feedback: Report it. Also: discuss a family code word with everyone today.

choices.text: Try to scam them back by sending a fake payment request
choices.feedback: Trying to 'scam back' a scammer is illegal, dangerous, and never works. They are professionals who have done this thousands of times. You risk losing more money or facing legal trouble yourself. Report to 1930 and your bank.

display.message: URGENT: Your mobile number has been reported for misuse. It will be disconnected in 2 hours. Call 09876-543210 to register your complaint and prevent disconnection.

choices.text: Call 09876-543210 to prevent disconnection
choices.feedback: That number connects directly to scammers who will ask for your Aadhaar, bank details, and eventually an OTP. TRAI does not send disconnection notices via SMS. The sender 'VM-TRAISS' is fake -- TRAI's sender ID would be 'TRAI' or from official DoT systems.

choices.text: Ignore, TRAI disconnection notices don't work like this
choices.feedback: Correct. TRAI does not text individuals about disconnection. Telecom operators send official notices, not random 10-digit numbers. The 2-hour urgency is classic Fear + Urgency. Your phone is fine.

choices.text: Forward to your telecom operator's official number to check
choices.feedback: Smart verification step. Your operator will confirm it is fake. Jio: 199 | Airtel: 121 | Vi: 199.

nodes.narrative: The call connects. A serious voice begins a lengthy script about your number being 'flagged for 2,847 illegal messages.' They ask for your Aadhaar and an OTP. You are now in a vishing call -- a live scam.

choices.text: Hang up immediately. TRAI does not operate this way.
choices.feedback: Correct exit. Never too late to hang up.

choices.text: Stay on the call and give them your Aadhaar to 'clear your name'
choices.feedback: Sharing your Aadhaar number on a scam call gives them a key piece of your identity. Combined with other leaked data, they can attempt SIM swaps, open fake accounts, or commit identity theft in your name. Hang up immediately.

display.message: Bhai, join our exclusive trading group. Our members made Rs 45,000 last month with just Rs 10,000 investment. Today is the last day for this month's batch. DM me NOW. Rs 500 joining fee only. Screenshot proof below.
display.attachment: A screenshot showing a trade app with 'Profit: Rs 45,230' in green

nodes.prompt: The screenshot looks convincing. What do you do?

choices.text: Pay Rs 500 to join, seems like a small risk for big potential
choices.feedback: There is no 'small risk' entry fee to legitimate trading. The screenshot is trivially easy to fake -- anyone can Photoshop a green number. Rs 500 is the first payment. Next comes Rs 5,000 for 'premium access,' then more.

choices.text: Ignore and report the account
choices.feedback: Perfect. This is a classic social media investment recruitment scam. Report @wealthwithsunilji to Instagram -- it protects others too. Any 'guaranteed profit' screenshot from an unknown account is bait.

choices.text: Ask for their SEBI registration number before paying
choices.feedback: Smart. They will not have one (or will send a fake). No SEBI registration = no money. Legitimate investment advisors are always registered and display their number openly.

nodes.narrative: You pay Rs 500. You are added to a WhatsApp group with 247 members cheering daily 'profits.' A week later, Sunil DMs you: 'Bhai, premium tier is Rs 7,000 for the real strategies. Your Rs 500 trial is expiring.' The group members are bots.

choices.text: Stop here, report to cybercrime.gov.in and don't pay further
choices.feedback: Correct exit. Rs 500 lost. Do not add Rs 7,000 to it.

choices.text: Pay the Rs 7,000 for premium access -- you might recover your Rs 500 through the 'real strategies'
choices.feedback: This is exactly how investment scams escalate. The Rs 500 is gone. The Rs 7,000 will also vanish. Then there will be a Rs 15,000 'VIP tier.' Each payment makes it harder to walk away because you keep thinking you can recover the previous loss. Stop now.

display.notification: Your Fixed Deposit of Rs 50,000 is maturing on 28-Mar. Would you like to renew? Log in to your HDFC app to choose renewal options.

nodes.prompt: You do have an FD at HDFC. What do you do?

choices.text: Open the HDFC app yourself (not from a link in the notification) and check FD options
choices.feedback: Excellent instinct. Opening the app yourself (not tapping any link) is exactly right. This notification is legitimate, but building the habit of navigating to apps yourself, rather than tapping notification links, keeps you safe even when a notification might be fake.

choices.text: Tap 'Log in' from the notification directly
choices.feedback: In this case the notification is legitimate. But as a habit, opening apps yourself is safer than tapping notification links. Fake app notifications can redirect to phishing pages.

choices.text: Ignore, FDs auto-renew anyway
choices.feedback: Technically fine if your FD is set to auto-renew. But checking your options is always better than missing a chance to redirect to higher-yield investments.

nodes.narrative: Two days pass. You check your bank statement hoping the money reappeared. It did not. The scammer has already withdrawn your Rs 5,000 and closed the account. Because you waited, the bank cannot freeze the destination account. The money is gone.

choices.text: File a late report on cybercrime.gov.in anyway -- it still helps catch repeat offenders
choices.feedback: Better late than never, but your recovery chances have dropped significantly. Always report within the first 30 minutes.

choices.text: Give up entirely and consider it a life lesson
choices.feedback: Understandable frustration, but even a late report helps. Your complaint adds to a pattern that helps authorities catch this scammer when they target others. File at cybercrime.gov.in. It takes 10 minutes.

nodes.narrative: You call back. The scammer picks up: 'Sir, we are processing your refund. Please share the new OTP we are sending to complete the reversal.' Another OTP arrives. You have walked into a second trap.

choices.text: Hang up and call HDFC's real helpline at 1800-202-6161
choices.feedback: You narrowly avoided a second loss. Scammers always have a follow-up script ready for people who call back. Never call a scammer's number -- only use official helplines.

choices.text: Share the new OTP since you need the reversal
choices.feedback: A second OTP shared means a second transaction authorized. You have now lost Rs 37,000 total. Each OTP you share is a separate transaction. Call your bank immediately at 1800-202-6161 and freeze everything.

nodes.narrative: You find 'CyberRecovery India' online, pay Rs 5,000 as their 'investigation fee.' They ask for your bank login 'to trace the transaction.' It is a secondary scam. You have now lost Rs 23,500 total and shared even more banking details with criminals.

choices.text: Stop everything and call HDFC directly at 1800-202-6161
choices.feedback: Two painful lessons in one day. Recovery services found via Google are almost always scams. The only legitimate recovery path is your bank + 1930 + cybercrime.gov.in.

choices.text: Change all your banking passwords immediately and then call 1930
choices.feedback: Good thinking on the password change since you shared credentials with a fake recovery service. But call your bank first to freeze your account -- password changes alone are not enough if they already have your details.

nodes.narrative: You reply to the fake Amazon email: 'Please reverse my transaction.' They respond: 'We need your UPI PIN and registered mobile number to process the reversal.' Replying has confirmed your email is active. You start receiving more phishing emails daily.

choices.text: Stop replying, mark as spam, and report on cybercrime.gov.in
choices.feedback: Never engage with scam emails. Replying confirms you are a real, responsive target. Block, report, and move on.

choices.text: Reply asking them to prove they are Amazon first
choices.feedback: Every reply gives scammers more information about you and confirms your email is active. They will craft increasingly convincing responses. Stop all contact. Block and report.

nodes.narrative: You send a collect request to the scammer's UPI ID for Rs 15,000. They screenshot your request and threaten to file a police complaint against YOU for harassment. You are now both out Rs 15,000 and being threatened by criminals.

choices.text: Stop all contact with the scammer and report everything to 1930
choices.feedback: Attempting to fight scammers on your own only makes things worse. Let the authorities handle it through proper channels. Report to 1930, your bank, and cybercrime.gov.in.

choices.text: Block the scammer's number and report the fraud to your bank
choices.feedback: Blocking is good but not sufficient. Also call 1930 and file at cybercrime.gov.in. The scammer's threat of a police complaint against you is empty -- you are the victim here.

nodes.narrative: You share your Aadhaar number. The 'officer' now has your name, phone number, and Aadhaar. Three days later, your phone loses signal. Someone has used your Aadhaar to attempt a SIM swap. Your OTPs are now going to a stranger's phone.

choices.text: Rush to your telecom store with original ID to reclaim your number
choices.feedback: Sharing your Aadhaar on a scam call can lead to identity theft, SIM swaps, and unauthorized account access. Lock your Aadhaar biometrics immediately at myAadhaar.uidai.gov.in.

choices.text: Call your bank from a family member's phone and freeze your accounts
choices.feedback: Smart priority -- securing your bank accounts first while your SIM is compromised. Then visit the telecom store with your original ID to reclaim your number. Also lock your Aadhaar biometrics at myAadhaar.uidai.gov.in.

nodes.narrative: You pay Rs 7,000. The 'premium group' has the same fake screenshots. Two weeks later, Sunil DMs again: 'Bhai, VIP tier is Rs 15,000 for the algo bot.' The rabbit hole has no bottom. You have lost Rs 7,500 total with zero real returns.

choices.text: Stop all payments and report to cybercrime.gov.in
choices.feedback: Investment scams are designed to escalate. Each payment makes the next one feel more justified -- 'I have already invested so much.' This is the sunk cost fallacy in action. Cut your losses now.

choices.text: Pay the Rs 15,000 VIP fee -- at this point, you need to recover what you have already lost
choices.feedback: This is exactly the sunk cost fallacy that investment scammers exploit. You have lost Rs 7,500. Paying Rs 15,000 more will not recover it -- it will make your total loss Rs 22,500. The 'algo bot' does not exist. Stop now and report to cybercrime.gov.in.

nodes.narrative: Your phone buzzes one last time. A message from Chip: 'That was a LOT for one Wednesday morning. But you handled it. You spotted the fake OTP call. You flagged the Amazon email. You did not scan the mystery QR. You protected your grandmother (or learned why you should). You are genuinely hard to scam now. That is not nothing -- most people do not figure this out until it costs them money.' Scam Spotter badge: unlocked.
nodes.timeSkip: 4:45 PM - end of the longest Wednesday
nodes.scoreMessage: Elite Scam Spotter. You caught everything that mattered.

nodes.narrative: Evening. You survived Wednesday relatively intact -- a few close calls, but no major losses. Chip gives you a cautious thumbs up: 'You did okay. A couple of spots where you hesitated when you should have been certain, but okay. The fact that you are thinking about this stuff at all puts you ahead of 80% of people. Keep sharpening.' Some badges unlocked. Some lessons reinforced.
nodes.scoreMessage: Good Spotter. A few close calls, but you held your ground.

nodes.narrative: It has been a rough Wednesday. Some money was lost. Some decisions did not land right. Chip pulls up a chair: 'Look, you got hit. It happens -- these people are professionals. The important thing is you know exactly what went wrong and why. And now you do. You will not make those same calls again. That is what this chapter was for.' Recovery guidance unlocked. File those reports.
nodes.scoreMessage: Learning Mode. Some hits taken, but every lesson is locked in now.

content.scenario: You get a call: 'Congratulations! Your mobile number has been selected in the Jio 25th Anniversary Mega Lucky Draw. You have won Rs 7,50,000 and a Samsung phone. To claim your prize, pay Rs 2,100 as GST processing fee via UPI to this number: 9876XXXXXX. Prize will be delivered in 24 hours.'

options.text: Pay the Rs 2,100, GST is legitimate and Rs 7.5 lakh is worth it
Negotiate, ask if you can pay a smaller fee first to verify
Hang up, legitimate prizes never require upfront fees to claim
Ask them to send prize details on WhatsApp first, then decide

content.explanation: This is an advance fee scam. There is no Jio lucky draw. If you pay Rs 2,100, there will be more fees -- 'insurance,' 'customs,' 'delivery charges' -- until you stop paying. The prize never arrives. The rule is absolute: real prizes do not require payment to claim. GST on prizes is deducted by the organizer, never collected upfront from the winner. Hang up. If you are tempted, Google 'Jio lucky draw' -- you will find no such thing exists.

content.scenario: WhatsApp message from +91 7834XXXXXX: 'Dear SBI Customer, your KYC has expired. Your account will be frozen in 24 hours. Update now: [link]. SBI Bank Team.' The link goes to 'sbi-kyc-update2024.in'.

options.text: Click the link, KYC expiry is a real thing banks ask about
Forward to your parents to check if their SBI KYC is up to date too
Delete and report, SBI communicates KYC through official app/registered mail, never WhatsApp links
Click only if you do have an SBI account

content.explanation: Three dead giveaways: (1) WhatsApp is not how banks send official KYC notices. (2) The domain 'sbi-kyc-update2024.in' is fake -- SBI's real domain is onlinesbi.sbi. (3) Random mobile numbers do not represent SBI. The link would take you to a phishing page that harvests your login credentials. Never click banking links from WhatsApp. If your KYC actually needs updating, you would see a notice in the SBI YONO app or receive physical mail.

content.scenario: You called Google Pay's 'customer care' number (found via Google Search) about a failed transaction. A helpful-sounding person says: 'Sir, I can see your payment is stuck. Please install AnyDesk on your phone so I can remotely process the reversal from our end. It will take 5 minutes.'
content.prompt: You really do have a stuck transaction. What should you do?

options.text: Install AnyDesk, you called them, so it must be legitimate
Install but don't share the screen access code
Hang up, Google Pay has no phone support; that number was a scammer's paid ad
Install but watch carefully to make sure they don't open your banking apps

content.explanation: Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm do NOT have customer care phone numbers you can call -- support is in-app only. The number you called via Google was a paid ad placed by scammers. This is real and documented. AnyDesk gives them your entire screen, including any OTPs that pop up. Once installed, they see everything. The stuck transaction? They would have 'fixed' it by draining your account. For real payment issues: use the Help section inside the app.

content.setup: Your grandmother calls you at 10 AM, very frightened. A 'CBI officer' has been on the phone with her for 45 minutes. He says your grandfather's account was used for illegal transactions. He told her not to tell anyone -- 'this is a confidential investigation.'

nodes.narrative: Dadi is whispering on the phone. 'Beta, CBI officer baat kar rahe hain. Keh rahe hain Dada ka account band ho jayega. Unhone bola kisi ko batao nahi.' She sounds terrified.

choices.text: Tell Dadi to stay on with the 'officer' while you call CBI to verify
choices.feedback: Getting better, but the best response is to tell her to hang up immediately. The longer she stays on, the more psychological pressure builds.

choices.text: Tell Dadi immediately: this is a scam, hang up right now, I'm coming over
choices.feedback: Perfect. The 'don't tell anyone' instruction is the biggest red flag -- it is designed to isolate victims. Real CBI investigations involve written notices and in-person visits, never 45-minute phone calls. Your confidence here breaks the spell.

nodes.narrative: Dadi stays on. The 'officer' gets more aggressive: 'Tell that person to stay out of this investigation. You must cooperate alone or your husband will be arrested today.'

choices.text: Tell Dadi to hang up, this escalating pressure proves it's a scam
choices.feedback: You got there. Escalating threats are the final tell. Real investigations do not intensify because a family member called. Hang up, go over, reassure her.

choices.text: Call the local police station yourself to verify if there is actually a case
choices.feedback: Verifying with real police is smart, but tell Dadi to hang up FIRST. Every extra minute on that call increases the scammer's psychological hold. Local police will confirm there is no such case.

nodes.narrative: Dadi hangs up. You go over. She is shaken but fine. Together, you register a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in for the attempt. Chip: 'You protected your family today. That matters more than any investment return.'
